transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Nimbus Head of ML), Aisha Khan (Nimbus Platform Eng), Liam O'Neill (Nimbus CTO)

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm jordan from redwood, maya's with me, we'll run through some edge case demos today 
d long context, high tps, streaming backpressure and timeouts. quick intros?
[00:18] Carlos: yeah hi carlos here, head of ml at nimbus, we're looking at replacing our current inference infra, goal is to support docs up to ~64k tokens and also sustain high throughput for real-time features.
[00:29] Aisha: aisha, platform eng, i'll be responsible for networking and peering, also care about egress and kms.
[00:36] Liam: liam here, cto, mostly listening for risk and cost tradeoffs.
[00:42] Jordan: great. maya you wanna kick off with the long context demo?
[00:46] Maya: sure, so first, very quick architecture note: redwood runtime uses a continuous batching layer and kv cache for long prefix reuse, that lets us serve 32k+ contexts without full re-encode every time, we also have kernel selection and quantization paths. right now i'll share my screen 
d slide deck link in chat (see demo slide).
[01:12] Maya: ok i'm pasting an example payload 
d it's a 64k token doc plus a short query at the end; pay attention to latency here, you'll see we stream partial token blocks while kv is warming so UX feels snappy even on large contexts.
[01:45] Carlos: quick question: when you say stream partial blocks, do you break the output into multiple streaming frames or do you buffer server side until completion? i've seen vendors that buffer and then stream which kills perceived latency.
[01:58] Maya: good call 
d we stream incremental chunks as soon as tokens are ready. under the hood there's an adaptive prefetch: if KV cache hits are low we pre-warm likely segments; if high-tps arrives we batch across requests but keep per-client latency SLOs by prioritizing small interactive requests.
[02:20] Aisha: what's the memory footprint for a 64k KV cache entry? we plan to serve multiple tenants per box.
[02:28] Maya: depends on model and quant; roughly [redacted] for our 32/64-bit baseline it's X GB per shard, with quantized 8-bit paths it's ~0.4X, we expose recommended instance types in the console when you select model+context. i'll show the console now.
[02:45] [03:00] Screen share: Console -> Model Config -> Context sizing table
[03:12] Maya: here the console suggests a dedicated pool of N GPUs for sustainable 5-10k tps for this workload; note that for multitenant hosted we route by policy and can fallback to smaller variants when capacity is constrained.
[03:34] Liam: fallback to smaller variants 
d are those distillations or lower context models? how do you keep semantics consistent?
[03:42] Jordan: usually model variants are same-arch quant/precision variants or shorter-context checkpoints. routing policies include quality thresholds and automated rollback if evals fall below the baseline.
[03:55] Carlos: ok let's pivot to the high tps demo 
d maya run the synthetic load?
[04:00] Maya: i'll kick a 10k rps synthetic workload from our load harness hitting three routes: 1) short interactive chat, 2) long-context doc search, 3) streaming completion for thin-client UI. watch the 'throughput' and 'latency p95' charts.
[04:30] [04:30] (demo runs)
[04:45] Maya: we see throughput ramped to ~9.6k rps, p95 for short requests stayed ~120ms due to prioritization and hot-shard caching; long-context p95 rose to ~1.8s as expected.
[05:02] Carlos: that's pretty good. but what happens when backpressure hits 
d e.g., spike that exceeds queues and triggers timeouts on mobile clients?
[05:12] Maya: we implement head-of-line protection and multi-queue scheduling: short interactive queues prioritized, long-context goes to background pool. streaming backpressure is handled by chunked sends plus a server-side backpressure window; if client's TCP or websocket buffer can't keep up we can pause send and buffer up to a configured limit, beyond that we apply graceful degradation 
d partial responses + explicit 'truncated' flag.
[05:40] Aisha: truncated flag 
d does the SDK expose that so clients can retry the rest of the stream? also how do you recommend retries to avoid thundering herd?
[05:52] Maya: yes SDK surfaces metadata: partial=true, cursor/token index for resume. We recommend exponential backoff with jitter and server-side retry tokens; for high tps pilots we commonly gate retry counts and use circuit breakers per client IP or API key.
[06:12] Liam: any observed impact on cost with aggressive retries?
[06:18] Jordan: retries increase token compute but Optimize suggestions can reduce unit cost 
d e.g., batching, prefix caches, and quantization suggestions. We showed a sample Optimize run earlier in the console that recommended switching to 8-bit quant for the long-context route saving ~35% cost with negligible eval regression for your workload.
[06:40] Carlos: Interesting. on the networking side 
d VPC and private deployment 
d can we run Dedicated on our VPC with customer-managed KMS?
[06:49] Maya: yes, Redwood Private (Dedicated) supports VPC peering or private link; KMS integration (bring-your-own KMS/HSM) is supported and audit logs available via our console or pushed to your S3/syslog.
[07:05] Aisha: and SSO? role-based access?
[07:08] Jordan: SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC with fine-grained roles, and token-level audit trails. we'll share SOC2 evidence after the call.
[07:18] [07:30] (Demo: intentional timeout scenario)
[07:32] Maya: now i'll simulate a client-side aggressive timeout of 300ms while a 2s long-context completion is streaming. you'll see the SDK resume token and how the server marks the stream truncated; also how the console shows a 'client timeout' event and traces the request across the runtime.
[08:00] Carlos: does the server keep computing for a timed-out connection or cancel compute?
[08:06] Maya: configurable 
d default is to continue compute for N seconds to allow soft-resume, but you can set cancel-on-timeout for strict cost control. For audits we log cancellation reason and partial output hash.
[08:24] Aisha: how are timeouts priced 
d if compute continues after client disconnects do you bill?
[08:30] Jordan: yes compute is billed; in Dedicated pilots we can provide billing controls and hard caps; Optimize will flag cost hotspots.
[08:40] Liam: what about graceful degradation for routing when a region loses capacity?
[08:45] Maya: smart routing will failover to another region or model variant per policy; we also support automatic degraded mode where we reply with cached answers from prefix cache for certain intents and mark them as 'cached' in the response.
[09:02] Carlos: any real world cases of this?
[09:06] Maya: we had a retailer pilot where a region outage led to 20% fallback to cached responses for product lookup paths, user experience had minor regressions but uptime stayed high.
[09:20] [09:40] (Question: integration and benchmarks)
[09:42] Carlos: can you share the harness and exact scenarios you ran so we can reproduce?
[09:47] Maya: yes 
d action item: i'll upload the load harness and a sample JMeter/locust config and a script that generates long-context payloads and record answers to the spreadsheet link.
[09:58] Jordan: we'll also provide a sample pilot contract and pricing bands for Dedicated fleet sizes.
[10:05] Aisha: for the 48-hour pilot 
d can you do a synthetic run that simulates our mix: 70% short chat, 20% long-context search, 10% streaming completions?
[10:13] Maya: yep we can seed the harness with that distribution; we'll also advise on warm-up sequence to pre-populate KV cache across shards.
[10:20] Liam: security checklist 
d can you confirm data residency options and retention?
[10:26] Jordan: data residency per region, retention windows configurable per-tenant, and logs can be delivered to your S3 for audits. SOC2 and ISO docs will be shared.
[10:35] Carlos: one more question: latency SLOs with packing/batching 
d do you ever observe headroom loss when many medium-size requests pack together?
[10:46] Maya: packing increases throughput efficiency but can increase p95 if not bounded; we provide packing thresholds in the console, and our routing prioritizes known interactive routes to bypass large packing windows.
[10:58] [11:20] (wrap-up)
[11:22] Jordan: ok recap 
d we'll: 1) share benchmark harness and sample payloads (maya), 2) send security/SOC2 docs (jordan), 3) propose Dedicated pricing and pilot template (jordan), 4) nimbus to provide anonymized long-context dataset and confirm VPC details (carlos/aisha).
[11:45] Carlos: sounds good, would also like the quantization eval report for our model family.
[11:50] Maya: we'll run a quantization eval and include the results in the shared sheet.
[11:56] Liam: thanks everyone, looking forward to the pilot.
[12:00] Jordan: thanks all, we'll follow up in the next 48 hours.

Notes: transcript contains occasional ASR mistakes and name misalignments (e.g., 'nimbus' misheard as 'num bus' in a couple timestamps). References to 'X GB' are redacted placeholders in the transcript for demo brevity.
